# Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta (MN 11 (PTS MN i 63))

**ID:** MN 11 (PTS MN i 63)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 63
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar", MN 11) is the eleventh discourse of the Majjhimanikāya and the opening sutta of the *Sīhanādavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Delivered at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, the sutta records the Buddha's bold assertion that genuine recluses representing the four stages of awakening are found solely within his dispensation [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. He explains that while other contemplative traditions may recognize and renounce attachment to sensual pleasures, views, and rules or observances, they fail to transcend grasping at a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*) [Anālayo 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse also discusses the eradication of clinging and the attainment of non-return when clinging remains with residue (*sa-upādisese*) [Anālayo 2010].

Horner, and Suddhāso Bhikkhu [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

Full parallels are preserved in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 103), the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 27.2), and the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 4.241). In comparative studies, Anālayo points out that where the Pali version specifies grasping at a "doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*), the Chinese parallels and a Sanskrit fragment parallel speak directly of clinging to "a self" (*ātmopādāna*) [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2017; Bingenheimer 2018].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: EA 27.2; MA 103 師子吼
- Passage-level parallels: AN 4.241 Samaṇasutta
